title: Drain a Worker Without Breaking Anything
description:
**SITUATION:**

`ds-spark-03` needs to come out for maintenance. Standalone Spark has no built-in graceful-drain command — decommissioning safely means designing around that gap: finish or relocate work without task failures, then prove you did not recreate the Lab 1.6 overcommit on the worker that remains.

After a naive stop, relocated executors often pile onto `ds-spark-02` — the same host that was capped under shared-worker pressure in Lab 1.6. A drain that "succeeds" with zero failures can still leave the cluster one wave away from the same executor-loss incident.

**YOUR TASK:**

1. Drain `ds-spark-03` so running work finishes or relocates with zero task failures.
2. Observe where the relocated executors land — expect concentration on `ds-spark-02`.
3. Confirm the drain did not quietly recreate the Lab 1.6 overcommit on `ds-spark-02`.
4. Enforce a per-application executor concentration limit (or equivalent placement rule) if needed so the post-drain shape stays safe.
5. Record the drain sequence, relocation, overcommit check, and guardrail in the Investigation tab.

**SPEC:**

- Zero task failures during the drain.
- `ds-spark-03` is out of the live worker set (or equivalently decommissioned for this lab).
- Post-drain placement does not recreate the Lab 1.6 overcommit on `ds-spark-02`.
- You can show the concentration limit (or placement check) that keeps a single application from packing unsafely onto one worker.
- Investigation tab is complete — every field filled. Submit stays off until it is.

hints: Stopping a worker mid-stage is not a drain — watch for task failures and lost shuffle.
After relocation, count executors per worker per application against the Lab 1.6 capacity story.
Standalone has no native drain API; the safe sequence is something you design, then verify.
Fill the Investigation tab; Submit stays off until every field is filled.
